A01.question: How often does an NBFC have to refresh KYC details for a customer it has classified as high risk?
A01.text: Under para 42 of the Know Your Customer Directions, 2025, an NBFC must carry out periodic updation of KYC "at least once in every two years for high-risk customers" from the date of opening of the account / last KYC updation [1][2]. The NBFC may also specify in its approved internal KYC policy exceptional measures for periodic updation, such as a more frequent updation schedule than the minimum prescribed under para 6 [6].

A02.question: What is the deadline for uploading a customer's KYC records to CKYCR after opening an account?
A02.text:
According to para 63 of the Know Your Customer Directions, 2025, an NBFC must upload KYC records pertaining to new individual accounts opened on or after April 1, 2017, and accounts of Legal Entities (LEs) opened on or after April 1, 2021, to CKYCR in terms of the provisions of the Rules [1][2]. If an NBFC obtains additional or updated information from a customer, it must furnish that information to CKYCR "within seven days or within such period as may be notified by the Central Government" [3]. 

The provided sources do not specify a specific timeframe or deadline (in days) for uploading records immediately following the initial opening of an account.

A07.question: What does the NBFC owe the borrower if it is late in handing back property documents after the loan is repaid?
A07.text:
According to para 39 of the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025, if the delay in releasing original movable / immovable property documents beyond 30 days after full repayment/settlement is attributable to the NBFC, it must communicate the reasons for the delay and compensate the borrower at the rate of ₹5,000 for each day of delay [1][2]. 

Under para 40 of the Directions, in the event of loss or damage to original documents, the NBFC must also assist the borrower in obtaining duplicate/certified copies and bear the associated costs in addition to the daily compensation, with the delayed period penalty calculated after an additional time of 30 days (i.e., after a total period of 60 days) [1][5]. 

Furthermore, as stated in para 41 of the Directions, this compensation is without prejudice to the borrower's rights to obtain any other compensation under applicable law [5].

A08.question: How long must a Key Facts Statement remain valid?
A08.text: Under para 29 of the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025, for all retail and MSME term loan products extended by all NBFCs, a Key Facts Statement (KFS) must have a validity period of "at least three working days for loans having tenor of seven days or more, and a validity period of one working day for loans having tenor of less than seven days" [1][4]. The NBFC is bound by the terms of the loan indicated in the KFS if agreed to by the borrower during this validity period [1].

A09.question: Can penal charges be capitalised or added to the rate of interest?
A09.text: According to para 30 of the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025, penalty charged for non-compliance of material terms and conditions cannot be added to the rate of interest, as it must be treated as 'penal charges' and not levied in the form of 'penal interest' [3]. Additionally, there shall be no capitalisation of penal charges (i.e., no further interest computed on such charges), and fresh or additional penal charges cannot be levied on earlier outstanding penal charges [1][3]. However, this prohibition does not affect normal procedures for compounding of interest in the loan account, allowing the NBFC to charge interest on unpaid interest at the contracted rate till the date of remediation [3].

A10.question: Are collection agents allowed to phone borrowers early in the morning or late at night?
A10.text: No, collection agents are restricted from calling borrowers early in the morning or late at night [1][2]. Under para 100 of the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025, an NBFC and its agents are prohibited from "calling the borrower before 8:00 a.m. and after 7:00 p.m. for recovery of overdue loans," though this direction does not apply to microfinance loans [2][3]. For microfinance borrowers, para 91 of the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025 explicitly deems "calling the borrower before 9:00 a.m. and after 6:00 p.m." as a harsh method that an NBFC or its agent shall not engage in [1].

A12.question: Can an NBFC levy prepayment or late-payment charges on microfinance loans?
A12.text: According to para 81 of the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025, an NBFC shall not levy any pre-payment charge on microfinance loans [4]. Charges for delayed payment may be levied, but they must be applied on the overdue amount and not on the entire loan amount [4]. Furthermore, under para 61 of the Credit Facilities Directions, 2025, interest rates and other charges or fees on microfinance loans should not be usurious and are subjected to supervisory scrutiny by the Reserve Bank [3].

A14.question: Before declaring someone responsible for a fraud, what must the NBFC do to give them a chance to respond?
A14.text: Under para 6 of the Fraud Risk Management Directions, 2026, the Applicable NBFC must adhere to principles of natural justice by issuing a detailed Show Cause Notice (SCN) to the persons (including third-party service providers and professionals), entities, and their promoters / whole-time and executive directors against whom an allegation of fraud is being examined [1][2]. The SCN must provide complete details of the transactions, actions, or events on the basis of which declaration and reporting of a fraud is being contemplated [2]. Additionally, the Applicable NBFC must provide a reasonable time of "not less than 21 days" to the persons or entities on whom the SCN was served to respond [2].

A17.question: Can part of a senior executive's bonus be held back and paid later depending on risk?
A17.text: For NBFCs-Middle Layer (NBFCs-ML) and Upper Layer (NBFCs-UL), a certain portion of variable pay, as decided by the Board of the NBFC, may be deferred to the time horizon of the risks (para 35 of the Governance Directions) [1]. A18.question: How many days overdue is an account classified as SMA-2?
A18.text: According to para 18 of the Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025, an account is classified as SMA-2 when principal or interest payment or any other amount is wholly or partly overdue for "More than 60 days and up to 90 days" [5].

A19.text: An NBFC must report credit information, including classification of an account as SMA, to CRILC on all borrowers having an aggregate exposure of "₹5 crore and above with them, on a monthly basis", as specified in para 20 of the Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025 [1]. A20.question: When can an NPA loan account be upgraded back to standard?
A20.text: Under para 24 of the Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning Directions, 2025, loan accounts classified as NPAs may be upgraded to ‘standard’ asset only if the entire arrears of interest and principal are paid by the borrower [1][2]. For borrowers having more than one credit facility, upgradation is permitted only upon the repayment of entire arrears of interest and principal pertaining to all credit facilities (para 25 of the Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning Directions, 2025) [1][2]. For accounts classified as NPA or retained as NPA on restructuring, upgradation occurs only when all outstanding facilities perform satisfactorily during the 'specified period' by servicing principal and interest as per the terms of payment (para 191 of the Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025) [3]. In addition, project finance accounts downgraded to NPA due to DCCO non-compliance may be upgraded after satisfactory performance post actual DCCO under para 115, or upon successful implementation of a resolution plan provided no further deferment request for DCCO is received under para 116 of the Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025 [4][6].

A22.question: What is the maximum loan-to-value ratio for consumption loans against gold?
A22.text:
According to para 43 of the Credit Facilities Directions, 2025, the maximum LTV ratio for consumption loans against eligible collateral is determined by the total consumption loan amount per borrower as follows:
* 85 per cent for amounts ≤ ₹2.5 lakh [1][2]
* 80 per cent for amounts > ₹2.5 lakh & ≤ ₹5 lakh [1][2]
* 75 per cent for amounts > ₹5 lakh [2]

Under para 44 of the Credit Facilities Directions, 2025, this prescribed LTV ratio must be maintained on an ongoing basis throughout the tenor of the loan [2].

A24.question: Which smaller non-deposit taking NBFCs sit in the Base Layer under Scale Based Regulation?
A24.text:
Under para 10 of the Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation Directions, 2025, the Base Layer comprises non-deposit taking NBFCs "below the asset size of ₹1,000 crore" [1]. 

Additionally, the Base Layer includes NBFCs undertaking the following specific activities:
1. NBFC-Peer to Peer Lending Platform (NBFC-P2P) [1][5],
2. NBFC-Account Aggregator (NBFC-AA) [1][5],
3. Non-Operative Financial Holding Company (NOFHC) [1][5], and
4. NBFCs holding a Certificate of Registration as ‘Type I NBFC’ [5]. 

Furthermore, per para 15, NBFC-P2P, NBFC-AA, NOFHC, and Type I NBFCs will always remain in the Base Layer [3].

A03.question: What parameters should an NBFC use for risk categorisation of customers under the KYC Directions?
A03.text: According to para 20 of Chapter IV – Risk Management of the Know Your Customer Directions, 2025, an NBFC shall undertake risk categorisation based on parameters such as the customer’s identity, social / financial status, nature of business activity, information about the customer’s business and its location, geographical risk covering customers as well as transactions, type of products / services offered, delivery channel used for delivery of products / services, and types of transactions undertaken such as cash, cheque / monetary instruments, wire transfers, forex transactions, etc. [1][2]. While considering the customer’s identity, the NBFC may also factor in the ability to confirm identity documents through online or other services offered by issuing authorities [2].

A07.question: What does the NBFC owe the borrower if it is late in handing back property documents after the loan is repaid?
A07.text:
According to para 39 of the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025, if the delay in releasing original movable / immovable property documents beyond 30 days after full repayment/settlement of the loan is attributable to the NBFC, it must communicate the reasons for the delay to the borrower and compensate the borrower at the rate of ₹5,000 for each day of delay [1][2]. 

Furthermore, under para 40 of the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025, in case of loss or damage to the original property documents (in part or in full), the NBFC must assist the borrower in obtaining duplicate/certified copies and bear the associated costs in addition to paying the daily compensation, with the delayed period penalty calculated after an additional 30 days (i.e., after a total period of 60 days) [1][5].

A09.question: Can penal charges be capitalised or added to the rate of interest?
A09.text: According to para 30 of the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025, penalty charged for non-compliance of material terms and conditions of a loan contract cannot be levied in the form of 'penal interest' that is added to the rate of interest charged on advances [3]. Furthermore, there shall be no capitalisation of penal charges (i.e., no further interest computed on such charges), and additional or fresh penal charges cannot be levied on the earlier outstanding amount of penal charges [1][3]. The NBFC is also prohibited from introducing any additional component to the rate of interest [1].

A10.question: Are collection agents allowed to phone borrowers early in the morning or late at night?
A10.text: No, NBFCs and their agents are prohibited from calling borrowers early in the morning or late at night. Under para 100 of the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, NBFCs and their agents are strictly barred from resorting to harassment, which includes "calling the borrower before 8:00 a.m. and after 7:00 p.m. for recovery of overdue loans," though this direction is not applicable to microfinance loans [2][3]. For microfinance borrowers, under para 91 of the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, "calling the borrower before 9:00 a.m. and after 6:00 p.m." is deemed a harsh method of recovery and is not permitted [1].

A20.question: When can an NPA loan account be upgraded back to standard?
A20.text: According to para 24 of Chapter II of the Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning Directions, 2025, loan accounts classified as NPAs may be upgraded to ‘standard’ assets only if the entire arrears of interest and principal are paid by the borrower [2]. For borrowers having more than one credit facility, loan accounts shall be upgraded from NPA to standard only upon repayment of the entire arrears of interest and principal pertaining to all the credit facilities (para 25 of the Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning Directions, 2025) [1][2]. Additionally, restructured accounts shall be upgraded only when all outstanding loans/facilities in the account perform satisfactorily during the 'specified period' (para 191 of Chapter XI of the Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025) [3]. For project finance accounts downgraded to NPA due to DCCO non-compliance, upgradation is permitted either after satisfactory performance post actual DCCO or on successful implementation of a resolution plan without further deferment requests (paras 115 and 116 of the Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025) [4][6].

A22.question: What is the maximum loan-to-value ratio for consumption loans against gold?
A22.text:

A03.question: What parameters should an NBFC use for risk categorisation of customers under the KYC Directions?
A03.text:
Under para 20(3) of Chapter IV – Risk Management of the Know Your Customer Directions, 2025, an NBFC shall undertake risk categorisation based on parameters such as:
- The customer’s identity [2]
- Social / financial status [2]
- Nature of business activity [2]
- Information about the customer’s business and its location [2][3]
- Geographical risk covering customers as well as transactions [2][3]
- Type of products / services offered [2][3]
- Delivery channel used for delivery of products / services [3]
- Types of transactions undertaken such as cash, cheque / monetary instruments, wire transfers, forex transactions, etc. [3]

Additionally, while considering the customer’s identity, the NBFC may factor in the ability to confirm identity documents through online or other services offered by issuing authorities [3].

A07.question: What does the NBFC owe the borrower if it is late in handing back property documents after the loan is repaid?
A07.text: According to para 39 of the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025, if a delay in releasing original movable / immovable property documents beyond 30 days after full repayment/ settlement of loan is attributable to the NBFC, it shall compensate the borrower at the rate of ₹5,000 for each day of delay [1][2]. In case of loss or damage to the original property documents, the NBFC must assist the borrower in obtaining duplicate/certified copies and bear the associated costs in addition to paying the daily compensation, with the penalty calculated after an additional 30 days (i.e., after a total period of 60 days) as per para 40 of the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025 [2][3]. Furthermore, under para 41 of the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025, this compensation is without prejudice to the borrower's rights to get any other compensation under any applicable law [3].

A14.text: According to para 6 of the Fraud Risk Management Directions, 2026, the Applicable NBFC must issue a detailed Show Cause Notice (SCN) to the Persons, Entities, and their Promoters / Whole-time and Executive Directors against whom fraud allegations are being examined, providing complete details of the transactions, actions, or events based on which declaration and reporting of a fraud is contemplated [2][3]. Furthermore, the Applicable NBFC must provide a reasonable time of "not less than 21 days" to the Persons / Entities on whom the SCN was served to respond [3].

A16.text: According to para 21 of the Compliance Function Directions, 2026, the Chief Compliance Officer (CCO) shall be appointed for a fixed minimum tenure of "not less than three years" [2]. A18.question: How many days overdue is an account classified as SMA-2?
A18.text: An account is classified as SMA-2 when the principal or interest payment or any other amount is wholly or partly overdue for "more than 60 days and up to 90 days" as set out in para 18 of the Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025 [2]. This SMA classification applies to all loans (including retail loans) irrespective of the size of exposure of the NBFC (para 19 of the Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025) [2][3].

A19.question: Which borrowers must an NBFC report to CRILC, and how often?
A19.text: According to para 20 of the Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025, an NBFC must report credit information, including classification of an account as SMA, to the Central Repository of Information on Large Credits (CRILC) on all borrowers having an aggregate exposure of ₹5 crore and above with them on a monthly basis [2]. Additionally, under para 21 of the same Directions, an NBFC must submit a weekly report of instances of default by all borrowers with an aggregate exposure of ₹5 crore and above by close of business on every Friday, or the preceding working day if Friday happens to be a holiday [2].

A20.question: When can an NPA loan account be upgraded back to standard?
A20.text:
According to para 24 of the Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning Directions, 2025, loan accounts classified as NPAs may be upgraded as a ‘standard’ asset only if entire arrears of interest and principal are paid by the borrower [2][3]. 

In the case of borrowers having more than one credit facility, para 25 provides that loan accounts shall be upgraded from NPA to standard asset category only upon repayment of entire arrears of interest and principal pertaining to all the credit facilities [3]. 

Additionally, as specified in paras 22 and 26, an account cannot be upgraded merely as a result of rescheduling, restructuring, or non-achievement of date of commence of commercial operations (DCCO) unless it satisfies the conditions in the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 [1][2][3].

A21.question: What is a customer owed if a mistake in their credit information is not fixed within a month of complaining?
A21.text: According to para 35 of the Credit Information Reporting Directions, 2025, complainants are entitled to compensation of ₹100 per calendar day if their complaint is not resolved within a period of thirty calendar days from the date of the initial filing of the complaint by the complainant with a CI / CIC [1][2]. Furthermore, a CI is required to pay compensation if it fails to send updated credit information to the CICs within 21 calendar days of being informed [3].

A22.question: What is the maximum loan-to-value ratio for consumption loans against gold?
A22.text:
According to para 43 of Chapter IV of the Credit Facilities Directions, 2025, the maximum Loan to Value (LTV) ratio for consumption loans against eligible collateral is determined by the total consumption loan amount per borrower:
- Up to ₹2.5 lakh (≤ ₹2.5 lakh): 85 per cent [2][3].
- Above ₹2.5 lakh and up to ₹5 lakh (> ₹2.5 lakh & ≤ ₹5 lakh): 80 per cent [2][3].
- Above ₹5 lakh (> ₹5 lakh): 75 per cent [3].

This prescribed LTV ratio must be maintained on an ongoing basis throughout the tenor of the loan as per para 44 [3].

A23.question: What minimum share of total assets must be qualifying assets for an NBFC-MFI?
A23.text: According to paragraph 12 of the Microfinance Institution Directions, 2025, qualifying assets of an NBFC-MFI shall constitute a minimum of 60 percent of the total assets (netted off by intangible assets), on an ongoing basis [2]. If an NBFC-MFI fails to maintain the qualifying assets for four consecutive quarters, it must approach the Reserve Bank with a remediation plan for taking a view in the matter [2].

A24.question: Which smaller non-deposit taking NBFCs sit in the Base Layer under Scale Based Regulation?
A24.text: Under para 10 of the Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation Directions, 2025, the Base Layer comprises "non-deposit taking NBFCs below the asset size of ₹1,000 crore" [2]. It also includes NBFCs undertaking specific activities, namely NBFC-Peer to Peer Lending Platform (NBFC-P2P), NBFC-Account Aggregator (NBFC-AA), Non-Operative Financial Holding Company (NOFHC), and NBFCs holding a Certificate of Registration as 'Type I NBFC' [2][3].
